claim: Myoglianin (Myo) is an Activin family member and a close homolog of mammalian Myostatin (Mstn).
source: Here, we demonstrate that Myoglianin (Myo), an Activin family member, and a close homolog of mammalian Myostatin (Mstn), is a muscle-derived extrinsic factor that uses canonical dSmad2-mediated signaling to regulate wing size.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by established knowledge of protein homology relationships.

claim: Myoglianin is a muscle-derived extrinsic factor.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Myoglianin (Myo), an Activin family member, and a close homolog of mammalian Myostatin (Mstn), is a muscle-derived extrinsic factor that uses canonical dSmad2-mediated signaling to regulate wing size.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing myo expression in muscles and rescue experiments demonstrating muscle-derived Myo affects disc growth.

claim: Myoglianin uses canonical dSmad2-mediated signaling to regulate wing size.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Myoglianin (Myo), an Activin family member, and a close homolog of mammalian Myostatin (Mstn), is a muscle-derived extrinsic factor that uses canonical dSmad2-mediated signaling to regulate wing size.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing loss of phospho-dSmad2 in myo mutants and genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: Myo is a myokine that helps mediate an allometric relationship between muscles and their associated appendages.
source: We propose that Myo is a myokine that helps mediate an allometric relationship between muscles and their associated appendages.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the experimental findings that muscle-derived Myo regulates imaginal disc growth.

claim: The Drosophila wing imaginal disc is a larval precursor to adult wings and thorax.
source: The Drosophila wing imaginal disc, the larval precursor to adult wings and thorax, has been widely used as a model to study the molecular mechanisms that control organ growth and size control (Martín et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge in Drosophila developmental biology, supported by citation.

claim: Dpp functions as a classic intrinsic morphogen in imaginal discs.
source: The Drosophila BMP ligand Decapentaplegic (Dpp) functions as a classic intrinsic morphogen, since it is secreted from a limited number of imaginal disc source cells and then diffuses throughout the tissue to regulate proliferation and patterning based on its concentration gradient (Campbell and Tomlinson, 1999; Lecuit et al., 1996; Restrepo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Activin-like signaling in Drosophila is initiated by three ligands: Myoglianin (Myo), Activinβ (Actβ), and Dawdle (Daw).
source: In Drosophila, Activin-like signaling is initiated by the three ligands, Myoglianin (Myo), Activinβ (Actβ), and Dawdle (Daw).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila TGFβ signaling pathway, supported by citation.

claim: Activin-like ligands bind to and activate a hetero-tetrameric receptor complex consisting of two type-I receptor subunits encoded by baboon (babo) and two type-II receptor subunits encoded by punt or wishful-thinking (wit).
source: These ligands bind to and activate a hetero-tetrameric receptor complex on the cell membrane consisting of two type-I receptor subunits encoded by the baboon (babo) locus and two type-II receptor subunits encoded by either the punt or wishful-thinking (wit) genes or perhaps a combination of the two (Upadhyay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Activated Babo phosphorylates cytosolic dSmad2 which then accumulates in the nucleus and regulates expression of target genes.
source: Activated Babo phosphorylates cytosolic dSmad2 which then accumulates in the nucleus and, along with the co-Smad Medea, regulates expression of target genes (Brummel et al., 1999; Hevia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There are three splice isoforms of babo with different ligand binding domains.
source: Notably, there are three splice isoforms of babo with different ligand binding domains, which presumably provide ligand binding specificity (Jensen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Babo null mutants die at the larval-pupal transition and have significantly smaller wing imaginal discs.
source: Babo null mutants die at the larval-pupal transition and have significantly smaller wing imaginal discs and escapers, produced by hypomorphic alleles, also have smaller adult wings (Brummel et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Expression of constitutively activated Babo in wing imaginal discs leads to larger adult wings that contain more cells.
source: Conversely, expression of constitutively activated Babo in wing imaginal discs leads to larger adult wings that contain more cells, suggesting that Activin-like signaling has a role in regulating proliferation (Brummel et al., 1999; Hevia and de Celis, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Babo can signal non-canonically through Mad to stimulate wing disc overgrowth in the background of a protein null allele of dSmad2.
source: Additionally, Babo can signal non-canonically through Mad (the BMP Smad) to stimulate wing disc overgrowth, but only in the background of a protein null allele of dSmad2 (Peterson and O'Connor, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Only myo mutants yield significantly smaller wing discs among the three Activin-like ligand mutants.
source: Interestingly, only myo mutants yield significantly smaller discs, phenocopying babo mutants. Myo wing discs are approximately 40% smaller than w1118 controls, but retain their normal shape and pattern (Figure 1B and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Myo wing discs are approximately 40% smaller than w1118 controls.
source: Myo wing discs are approximately 40% smaller than w1118 controls, but retain their normal shape and pattern (Figure 1B and E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Myo mutant wing discs retain their normal shape and pattern.
source: Myo wing discs are approximately 40% smaller than w1118 controls, but retain their normal shape and pattern (Figure 1B and E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1B.

claim: Actβ mutant discs had no significant size defects.
source: Actβ mutant discs had no significant size defects, while daw mutant discs were slightly smaller, which may be attributable to the reduction of insulin secretion in the daw mutants (Figure 1C-E; Ghosh and O'Connor, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Daw mutant discs were slightly smaller, which may be attributable to the reduction of insulin secretion in the daw mutants.
source: Actβ mutant discs had no significant size defects, while daw mutant discs were slightly smaller, which may be attributable to the reduction of insulin secretion in the daw mutants (Figure 1C-E; Ghosh and O'Connor, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work on daw function.

claim: Haltere and leg imaginal discs are also approximately ~40% smaller in myo mutants.
source: Indeed, both these imaginal discs are also approximately ~40% smaller in myo mutants and maintain their proportional size (Figure 1F-I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-I.

claim: Myo signaling regulates tissue growth in wing, haltere, and leg imaginal discs to similar extents.
source: This suggests that Myo signaling regulates tissue growth in all three of these imaginal discs to similar extents.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all three disc types show similar size reductions in myo mutants.

claim: Cells in myo mutant discs are approximately ~20% smaller than controls based on cell density measurements.
source: We calculated that the cells in these mutants are approximately ~20% smaller than controls (Figure 1J-L).
evidence: This is supported by phalloidin staining and cell density measurements shown in Figure 1J-L.

claim: There is no significant difference in the number of mitotic cells between myo mutant discs and controls at 90-96 hr AEL.
source: We examined proliferation by staining for phospho-Histone 3(ser10) to mark mitotic cells, and found no significant difference between myo discs and controls at this stage (Figure 1M-O).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-Histone H3 staining data shown in Figure 1M-O.

claim: There is no increase in apoptosis in myo mutant discs at 90-96 hr AEL.
source: Next, we stained 90–96 hr AEL discs with anti-cleaved-caspase 3, an apoptosis marker, and found no increase in apoptosis in myo mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, A–B).
evidence: This is supported by cleaved-caspase 3 staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: TOR signaling is not perturbed in myo mutant discs.
source: We found no decrease in pS6 staining in myo mutant discs, indicating that TOR signaling is not perturbed in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, C–D).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-S6 staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myo1 mutant muscles are 13% smaller vs heterozygote controls.
source: Surprisingly, myo1 mutant muscles are 13% smaller vs heterozygote controls (p=0.02), however they contain the same number of nuclei per fiber, which suggests that there were no defects in myoblast fusion during embryogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, P–S).
evidence: This is supported by muscle size measurements shown in Figure 1P-S.

claim: Myo1 mutant muscles contain the same number of nuclei per fiber as controls.
source: Surprisingly, myo1 mutant muscles are 13% smaller vs heterozygote controls (p=0.02), however they contain the same number of nuclei per fiber, which suggests that there were no defects in myoblast fusion during embryogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, P–S).
evidence: This is supported by nuclei counting data shown in Figure 1S.

claim: Drosophila myo is not functionally conserved with vertebrate Mstn in regulating muscle size.
source: Taken together our results suggest that Drosophila myo is not functionally conserved with vertebrate Mstn in regulating muscle size.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that myo mutants do not have larger muscles like vertebrate Mstn mutants.

claim: In homozygous myo null mutants there is no detectable phospho-dSmad2 signal in wing discs.
source: In homozygous null mutants there is no signal under our detection conditions. These findings indicate that Myo is the primary ligand for TGFβ/Activin signaling in wing discs (Figure 1T-U).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1T.

claim: Myo is the primary ligand for TGFβ/Activin signaling in wing discs.
source: These findings indicate that Myo is the primary ligand for TGFβ/Activin signaling in wing discs (Figure 1T-U).
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of phospho-dSmad2 signal in myo mutants.

claim: Baboon encodes three splice isoforms (Babo-A, Babo-B, and Babo-C) that differ only in their extracellular, ligand binding domains.
source: The three splice isoforms are a result of mutually exclusive alternative splicing of the fourth exon (4a, 4b, 4 c) giving rise to three receptors (Babo-A, Babo-B, and Babo-C) (Brummel et al., 1999; Jensen et al., 2009) that differ only in their extracellular, ligand binding domains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Only babo-a is expressed in late L3 wing discs based on qPCR analysis.
source: We isolated late L3 wing discs and performed qPCR analysis using isoform specific primers, and detected only babo-a expression in the discs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Knockdown of babo-a by esg-GAL4 results in 40% smaller adult wings.
source: In support of the qPCR data, we find that knocking down babo-a alone with esg-GAL4 results in 40% smaller adult wings, whereas knocking down babo-b or babo-c has no effect on wing size (Figure 2C-F, O).
evidence: This is supported by wing size measurements shown in Figure 2C-F, O.

claim: Knocking down babo-b or babo-c has no effect on wing size.
source: In support of the qPCR data, we find that knocking down babo-a alone with esg-GAL4 results in 40% smaller adult wings, whereas knocking down babo-b or babo-c has no effect on wing size (Figure 2C-F, O).
evidence: This is supported by wing size measurements shown in Figure 2C-F, O.

claim: Ci-GAL4 driving babo-a RNAi reduces the anterior compartment by 50%.
source: Using compartment specific GAL4 lines, we find that Ci-GAL4 driving babo-a RNAi reduces the anterior compartment by 50% (Figure 2F-I, L) G-J,O).
evidence: This is supported by compartment size measurements shown in Figure 2G-J, O.

claim: Knocking down babo-a in the posterior compartment using hh-GAL4 reduced the relative size of the compartment by 35%.
source: Similar to the other drivers, we observed that knocking down babo-a in the posterior compartment reduced the relative size of the compartment by 35% (Figure 2K-N, P).
evidence: This is supported by compartment size measurements shown in Figure 2K-N, P.

claim: Knockdown of babo-a using ci-GAL4 results in 13% increase in trichome density (smaller cells).
source: Knockdown of babo-a using esg-GAL4 does not affect trichome density, whereas ci-GAL4 result in a 13% increase in trichome density, i.e. smaller cells (Figure 2Q).
evidence: This is supported by trichome density measurements shown in Figure 2Q.

claim: Knocking down babo-a leads to an ~40% decrease in the epithelium thickness.
source: Using confocal optical sectioning we observed that knocking down babo-a leads to an ~40% decrease in the epithelium thickness (Figure 2K-N, (cross-section), R).
evidence: This is supported by epithelium thickness measurements shown in Figure 2K-N, R.

claim: Knocking down babo-a in the entire wing disc completely abolishes phospho-dSmad2 levels.
source: As predicted, knocking down babo-a in the entire wing disc by simultaneously using ci-GAL4 and hh-GAL4 completely abolishes phospho-dSmad2 levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2S.

claim: The level of phospho-Mad in wing discs is not changed when babo-a is knocked down.
source: Furthermore, the level of phospho-Mad in these discs is not changed (Figure 2T).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2T.

claim: Babo-A is the only functional isoform in the wing imaginal disc.
source: The data indicate that Babo-A is the only functional isoform in the wing imaginal disc and its removal phenocopies myo mutants in regulating wing disc growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only babo-a knockdown affects disc size and signaling.

claim: Myo signals solely through Babo-A in the wing imaginal disc.
source: Thus, similar to the mushroom body neurons (Awasaki et al., 2011), our data demonstrate that Myo signals solely through Babo-A in the wing imaginal disc.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined qPCR, RNAi, and signaling data, and supported by citation to similar findings in mushroom body neurons.

claim: Knocking down dSmad2 and babo-a simultaneously rescues brk reporter expression.
source: Knocking down dSmad2 and babo-a rescued brk reporter expression (Figure 3, A vs B), while RNAi of dSmad2 and babo-b or babo-c did not (Figure 3, A vs C-D).
evidence: This is supported by brk-LacZ reporter expression data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: RNAi for punt completely suppresses the dSmad2 RNAi induced brk silencing.
source: RNAi for wit does not rescue brk silencing (Figure 3, E vs G), however RNAi for punt completely suppresses the dSmad2 RNAi induced brk silencing (Figure 3, E vs H).
evidence: This is supported by brk-LacZ reporter expression data shown in Figure 3E-H.

claim: Babo-A requires Punt, but not Wit, for repression of brk expression in the non-canonical signaling assay.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that Babo-A requires Punt, but not Wit, for repression of brk expression in this non-canonical signaling assay and it is likely that the same receptors are used for Myo signaling in wild type disc cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic epistasis experiments with type II receptor RNAi.

claim: Myo-GAL4 drives expression in Repo+ glial cells of the brain and ventral ganglia, as well as larval body wall muscles.
source: We detect GFP expression in both Repo+ glial cells of the brain and the ventral ganglia, as well as the larval body wall muscles (Figure 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but not in any imaginal discs (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by myo-GAL4 driven GFP expression data shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myo-GAL4 does not drive detectable expression in imaginal discs.
source: We detect GFP expression in both Repo+ glial cells of the brain and the ventral ganglia, as well as the larval body wall muscles (Figure 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but not in any imaginal discs (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the absence of GFP signal in imaginal discs shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of myo in dSmad2 mutant background suppresses the dSmad2 overgrowth, resulting in small discs similar in size to myo mutants.
source: First, using null mutant alleles, we confirmed that loss of myo in dSmad2 mutant background suppresses the dSmad2 overgrowth, resulting in small discs similar in size to myo mutants (Figure 4C-E, L).
evidence: This is supported by disc size measurements shown in Figure 4C-E, L.

claim: Ubiquitous knockdown of myo using da-GAL4 suppresses wing disc overgrowth in dSmad2 mutants.
source: To confirm efficacy of the RNAi constructs, we first used the da-GAL4 driver to ubiquitously knock down myo in the dSmad2 background and confirmed that it suppresses wing disc overgrowth (Figure 4, F vs G, L).
evidence: This is supported by disc size measurements shown in Figure 4F-G, L.

claim: Knocking down myo using esg-GAL4 (wing disc) or repo-GAL4 (glia) failed to suppress the dSmad2 wing disc overgrowth.
source: However knocking down myo using either esg-GAL4 (wing disc) or repo-GAL4 (glia) failed to suppress the dSmad2 wing disc overgrowth (Figure 4, F vs H, I).
evidence: This is supported by disc size measurements shown in Figure 4F, H, I.

claim: RNAi knockdown of myo in body wall muscles using mhc-GAL4 or mef2-GAL4 completely suppresses the dSmad2 disc overgrowth phenotype.
source: In contrast, RNAi knockdown of myo in body wall muscles, using either mhc-GAL4 or mef2-GAL4 drivers, completely suppresses the dSmad2 disc overgrowth phenotype phenocopying the dSmad2;myo double mutant (Figure 4, F vs J, K).
evidence: This is supported by disc size measurements shown in Figure 4F, J, K, L.

claim: Muscles are the major source of Myo that stimulates imaginal disc growth.
source: Therefore, we conclude that muscles are the major source of Myo that stimulates imaginal disc growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific RNAi experiments showing only muscle-specific knockdown suppresses dSmad2 overgrowth.

claim: Overexpression of myo in larval muscles in wild type animals results in wings that are larger than normal.
source: First, overexpression of myo in larval muscles in wild type animals results in wings that are larger than normal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by wing size measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of myo in glia results in partial rescue of myo mutant disc size.
source: Overexpression in glia (repo-GAL4) results in partial rescue (Figure 5C and F) while overexpression in muscle (mef2-GAL4, Figure 5D and F) or fat body (cg-GAL4, Figure 5E and F) leads to complete rescue.
evidence: This is supported by disc size measurements shown in Figure 5C, F.

claim: Overexpression of myo in muscle leads to complete rescue of myo mutant disc size.
source: Overexpression in glia (repo-GAL4) results in partial rescue (Figure 5C and F) while overexpression in muscle (mef2-GAL4, Figure 5D and F) or fat body (cg-GAL4, Figure 5E and F) leads to complete rescue.
evidence: This is supported by disc size measurements shown in Figure 5D, F.

claim: Overexpression of myo in fat body leads to complete rescue of myo mutant disc size.
source: Overexpression in glia (repo-GAL4) results in partial rescue (Figure 5C and F) while overexpression in muscle (mef2-GAL4, Figure 5D and F) or fat body (cg-GAL4, Figure 5E and F) leads to complete rescue.
evidence: This is supported by disc size measurements shown in Figure 5E, F.

claim: Muscle-derived Myo acts as an endocrine-like ligand via the hemolymph to activate a specific receptor complex on disc cells.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that muscle-derived Myo acts as an endocrine-like ligand via the hemolymph to activate a specific receptor complex on disc cells, consisting of Babo-A and Punt, that signals to dSmad2 to promote imaginal disc growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of tissue-specific expression, knockdown, and rescue experiments.

claim: The receptor complex for Myo signaling in disc cells consists of Babo-A and Punt.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that muscle-derived Myo acts as an endocrine-like ligand via the hemolymph to activate a specific receptor complex on disc cells, consisting of Babo-A and Punt, that signals to dSmad2 to promote imaginal disc growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the receptor isoform and type II receptor experiments.

claim: Vertebrate Myostatin (Mstn) is notable for its role in regulating skeletal muscle mass.
source: Insect myoglianin is a clear homolog of vertebrate Myostatin (Mstn/GDF8) (Hinck et al., 2016), a TGFβ family member notable for its role in regulating skeletal muscle mass.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mstn loss-of-function mutants lead to enlarged skeletal muscles.
source: Mstn loss-of-function mutants lead to enlarged skeletal muscles (Grobet et al., 1997; McPherron and Lee, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mstn is thought to affect muscle size through autocrine signaling that limits muscle stem cell proliferation and by perturbing protein homeostasis via the Insulin/mTOR signaling pathways.
source: Mstn is thought to affect muscle size through autocrine signaling that limits muscle stem cell proliferation, as well as perturbing protein homeostasis via the Insulin/mTOR signaling pathways (Morikawa et al., 2016; Rodriguez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mstn and Gdf11 are found to circulate in the blood as latent complexes in which their N-terminal prodomains remain associated with the ligand domain.
source: Both molecules are found to circulate in the blood as latent complexes in which their N-terminal prodomains remain associated with the ligand domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate TGFβ ligands.

claim: Activation of Mstn and Gdf11 requires additional proteolysis of the N-terminal fragment by Tolloid-like metalloproteases.
source: Activation requires additional proteolysis of the N-terminal fragment by Tolloid-like metalloproteases to release the mature ligand for binding to its receptors (Uhlén et al., 2015; Wolfman et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Myoglianin N-terminal domain was found to be processed by Tolloid-like factors.
source: Interestingly in Drosophila, the Myoglianin N-terminal domain was also found to be processed by Tolloid-like factors, but whether this is a prerequisite for signaling has not yet been established (Serpe and O'Connor, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of Actβ results in smaller muscles.
source: Intriguingly however, we find that loss of Actβ, another ligand that signals through Babo and dSmad2, results in a smaller muscles (Moss-Taylor et al., 2019) contrary to that produced by loss of vertebrate Mstn and various other vertebrate Activin family members.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In Drosophila the Myo/Activin pathway promotes muscle growth while in vertebrates it inhibits muscle growth.
source: Thus, in Drosophila the Myo/Activin pathway promotes muscle growth while in vertebrates it inhibits muscle growth.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing Drosophila and vertebrate phenotypes.

claim: Dpp has been shown to be secreted into the hemolymph where it circulates and signals to the prothoracic gland to regulate a larval nutritional checkpoint.
source: Even the disc intrinsic molecule Dpp has been recently shown to be secreted into the hemolymph where it circulates and signals to the prothoracic gland to regulate a larval nutritional checkpoint (Setiawan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Muscle-derived Actβ and Myo signal to the fat body to regulate mitochondrial function and ribosomal biogenesis, respectively.
source: For example, muscle-derived Actβ and Myo signal to the fat body to regulate mitochondrial function and ribosomal biogenesis, respectively (Demontis et al., 2014; Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Daw produced from many tissue sources can signal to the Insulin producing cells and the midgut to stimulate Insulin secretion and repress expression of sugar metabolizing genes, respectively.
source: In addition, Daw produced from many tissue sources can signal to the Insulin producing cells and the midgut to stimulate Insulin secretion and repress expression of sugar metabolizing genes, respectively (Chng et al., 2014; Ghosh and O'Connor, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Larval muscles are histolysed during metamorphosis and do not contribute to the adult muscle.
source: Larval muscles are histolysed during metamorphosis and do not contribute to the adult muscle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Remnants of larval muscles in the thoracic segment are preserved as fibers that act as scaffolds upon which the larval myoblasts infiltrate and fuse to become the adult indirect flight muscles.
source: However, remnants of larval muscles in the thoracic segment are preserved as fibers that act as scaffolds upon which the larval myoblasts infiltrate and fuse to become the adult indirect flight muscles (Dutta et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Wg and Serrate/Notch signaling from the wing disc epithelial cells control myoblast proliferation during larval development.
source: Wg and Serrate/Notch signaling from the wing disc epithelial cells control myoblast proliferation during larval development (Gunage et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Motor neuron derived Actβ can dramatically affect muscle/body size.
source: We have recently demonstrated that in Drosophila, motor neuron derived Actβ, another TGFβ superfamily member, can dramatically affect muscle/body size (Moss-Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work by the authors.
